standard.title: Terminating and Recurring Decimals
standard.description: recognise terminating and recurring decimals, using digital tools as appropriate
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can convert fractions to decimals and understand that some fractions produce repeating decimals (from AC9M7N04). Students understand prime factorisation (from AC9M7N02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise terminating and recurring decimals and identify from the prime factorisation of the denominator whether a fraction produces a terminating decimal.

nodes.label: Identifying terminating and recurring decimals
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students distinguish terminating from recurring decimals and use correct notation for recurring decimals.
nodes.minimum_width: Classify given fractions as terminating or recurring by division; write recurring decimals using dot or bar notation.
nodes.typical_width: Identify terminating, recurring and non-terminating (irrational) decimals; use digital tools to explore the decimal expansion of fractions; apply correct notation.
wider: Investigate the length of the repeating cycle for unit fractions (1/7, 1/11, 1/13) and look for patterns — connect to divisibility.
Explore why 0.999... = 1 using the recurring decimal as an argument — discuss what this tells us about real number representation.

response_modes.reason: Students often believe all fractions terminate or that recurring means 'goes on forever randomly'. Multiple examples across different denominators resolve these misconceptions.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to predict termination from prime factorisation — students who cannot reliably classify a decimal as terminating or recurring by inspection cannot verify whether their prime factorisation prediction is correct.
success_criteria: Correctly classifies a fraction's decimal expansion as terminating or recurring.
Writes a recurring decimal using correct notation.
Does not confuse recurring with irrational (non-terminating, non-recurring).

nodes.label: Predicting termination from prime factorisation of denominator
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students identify whether a fraction terminates by examining whether the prime factorisation of the denominator contains only factors of 2 and/or 5.
nodes.minimum_width: State the rule and apply it to determine whether a given fraction terminates, without performing the division.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the rule across a range of fractions including those in non-simplest form; explain why denominators with only 2s and 5s produce terminating decimals.
wider: Investigate why only factors of 2 and 5 produce terminating decimals in base 10 — connect to the structure of our number system and how this would differ in base 12.
Explore mixed examples where simplification first is required before applying the rule.

response_modes.reason: The connection between prime factorisation and decimal behaviour requires an explicit logical chain that students rarely construct spontaneously. A scaffold linking the denominator structure to the decimal base is needed.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The connection to base 10 structure and how the rule would differ in other bases is genuinely rich for advancing students — it connects number theory to the arbitrary choices embedded in our numeration system.
success_criteria: Correctly predicts whether a fraction terminates from its denominator's prime factorisation.
Explains why the rule works (connection to base 10).
Simplifies fractions first where necessary before applying the rule.
